uni-bba-core-sem1.title: BBA Semester 1 core
uni-bba-core-sem1.description: First-semester BBA core: principles of management, financial accounting, business economics and business mathematics, with worked numericals, case scenarios and unit exams. Independent study companion; topic tags only.

courses.title: Principles of Management
courses.summary: Management as a discipline: Taylor, Fayol and Weber, the planning-organising-leading-controlling cycle, delegation, span of control, MBO and motivation theories, applied to realistic Indian workplace cases.
outcomes: Learners can contrast scientific, administrative and bureaucratic schools
Learners can write SMART objectives and run an MBO cycle
Learners can distinguish authority, responsibility and accountability in delegation
Learners can apply Maslow, Herzberg and McGregor to a case

lessons.title: Lab: Classical thinkers and what they got right

story.title: Two bosses at a Pune packaging unit

scenes.text: Plant head Sunil times every packing motion with a stopwatch and pays a bonus for beating the standard time.
Regional manager Neha instead asks what functions the plant needs: planning, organising, commanding, coordinating, controlling.
Both are borrowing from classical management theory, from different ends of the organisation.

steps.title: Scientific management (F. W. Taylor, 1911)
steps.body: Taylor looked at **the shop floor**: study each task, find the one best method, select and train workers scientifically, and link pay to output (differential piece rate). Strength: big productivity gains. Weakness: treats people as machines and ignores motivation beyond money.

steps.title: Administrative theory (Henri Fayol)
steps.body: Fayol looked at **top management**. He listed five functions (planning, organising, commanding, coordinating, controlling) and 14 principles, including division of work, authority and responsibility, unity of command, unity of direction, scalar chain, esprit de corps and initiative. Modern textbooks compress the functions into planning, organising, leading, controlling.

steps.title: Bureaucracy (Max Weber)
steps.body: Weber described an ideal bureaucracy: fixed hierarchy, written rules, specialised roles, impersonal relations, hiring on qualification. It gives predictability and fairness in large bodies such as government offices; the risk is red tape.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Taylor and Fayol are the same: Taylor is operations-level, Fayol is whole-organisation level.
- Calling unity of command and unity of direction the same: the first is one boss per employee, the second is one plan per group of activities.

lessons.title: Lab: Plan with SMART objectives and MBO

scenes.text: Kavya manages a 6-person sales team at a mobile accessories distributor. Her director says: do better this year.
Nobody knows what better means. Kavya converts it into numbers with each person.
They agree objectives, review quarterly and appraise against results: Management by Objectives.

steps.title: Planning in one line
steps.body: Planning decides **what to achieve and how**, ahead of time. Types: strategic (long term, top level), tactical (middle level, 1-3 years), operational (day-to-day). Steps: set objectives, scan the environment, develop alternatives, evaluate, choose, implement, review.

steps.title: MBO (Peter Drucker, 1954)
steps.body: Superior and subordinate **jointly** set objectives, define results expected, then use them to run the unit and appraise performance. Cycle: set organisational goals, set individual goals, monitor, evaluate, reward and reset. Works best with measurable goals; fails when goals are imposed or when it ignores quality.

steps.title: Worked example: a SMART objective
steps.body: Weak: increase sales. SMART: **Increase monthly sales of accessories in Zone B from 40 lakh to 46 lakh by 31 March**. Specific (zone, product), Measurable (lakh), Achievable (15% rise), Relevant (company growth), Time-bound (31 March). Growth = (46-40)/40 = 15%.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing activities (hold meetings) instead of results.
- Setting a goal the employee had no say in; that is not MBO.

activity.prompt: Is each statement a SMART objective or a vague wish?

scenes.text: Rohit, finance head, hands the vendor audit file to analyst Meera and goes on leave.
A wrong figure goes to the auditors. Rohit says it was Meera's job.
His CFO disagrees: you delegated the work, not your accountability.

steps.title: Authority, responsibility, accountability
steps.body:
- **Authority**: right to decide and command.
- **Responsibility**: duty to perform the assigned task.
- **Accountability**: answerability for the outcome. Authority and responsibility can be delegated; **accountability cannot be passed down** entirely, the superior stays answerable.

steps.title: Delegation steps and span of control
steps.body: Steps: assign duties, grant authority, create obligation, follow up. Span of control = number of subordinates a manager supervises directly. Narrow span gives tight control and tall hierarchy; wide span gives flat structure and faster decisions. Typical effective spans are 5-8 at senior levels and larger for routine work.

steps.title: Worked example: management layers
steps.body: An organisation has 500 operatives; each supervisor handles 10 people. Supervisors = 500/10 = 50. If each manager has a span of 5, managers = 50/5 = 10. If those 10 report to one head with span of 10, total levels above operatives = 3 (supervisor, manager, head).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Delegating authority without resources.
- Believing the delegate alone is blamed if things fail.

steps.title: Maslow, Herzberg, McGregor
steps.body: **Maslow**: physiological, safety, social, esteem, self-actualisation. **Herzberg**: hygiene factors (pay, policy, conditions) prevent dissatisfaction; motivators (recognition, achievement, growth) create satisfaction. **McGregor**: Theory X assumes people dislike work and need control; Theory Y assumes they seek responsibility.

steps.title: Diagnosis
steps.body: Pay is high, so the hygiene factor pay is fine. Complaints are recognition and autonomy: motivators missing, plus Theory X supervision. Best fixes: recognition programme, scripts with discretion, coach supervisors toward Theory Y.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Answering with a pay rise when pay is not the problem.
- Treating hygiene factors as motivators.

courses.title: Financial Accounting
courses.summary: The accounting equation, double entry, journal to trial balance, depreciation methods and basic ratio reading, with numerical practice.
outcomes: Learners can apply the accounting equation to transactions
Learners can pass journal entries with correct debit and credit
Learners can compute depreciation by straight-line and written-down-value methods
Learners can compute current ratio and gross profit margin

scenes.text: Aman starts Crumb and Co. with 5,00,000 of his own money and borrows 2,00,000 from a bank.
He buys an oven for 3,00,000 in cash and flour on credit for 40,000.
After each event the books must still balance.

steps.title: The equation
steps.body: **Assets = Liabilities + Owner's equity**. Every transaction changes at least two items and keeps both sides equal. Assets are resources owned (cash, stock, machinery); liabilities are obligations (loans, creditors); equity is the owner's claim (capital plus profits minus drawings).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
1. Capital 5,00,000 + loan 2,00,000: cash 7,00,000 = loan 2,00,000 + capital 5,00,000.
2. Oven bought for cash 3,00,000: cash 4,00,000 + oven 3,00,000 = 7,00,000 assets. Total unchanged.
3. Flour on credit 40,000: stock +40,000 and creditors +40,000. Assets 7,40,000 = liabilities 2,40,000 + equity 5,00,000.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating a loan received as income; it is a liability.
- Treating drawings as an expense; drawings reduce equity directly.

lessons.title: Lab: Journal entries and the trial balance

story.title: Three days in the bakery's books

scenes.text: Aman records: cash sale 25,000; rent paid 10,000; salary paid 8,000.
At month end the accountant lists every ledger balance.
If debit total equals credit total, the arithmetic is probably right.

steps.title: Debit and credit rules
steps.body: Modern rules: **Assets and expenses**: debit increases, credit decreases. **Liabilities, capital and income**: credit increases, debit decreases. Each journal entry has equal debits and credits.

steps.title: Entries
steps.body:
- Cash sale 25,000: Dr Cash 25,000; Cr Sales 25,000.
- Rent paid 10,000: Dr Rent 10,000; Cr Cash 10,000.
- Salary paid 8,000: Dr Salary 8,000; Cr Cash 8,000.
Cash balance from these = 25,000 - 10,000 - 8,000 = 7,000 (debit).

steps.title: What a trial balance proves
steps.body: Equal totals prove only arithmetic agreement. Errors of omission, compensating errors and entries to a wrong account of the right type do not show up.

steps.title: Two core ratios
steps.body: **Current ratio** = current assets / current liabilities (liquidity; rule of thumb about 2:1 but depends on industry). **Gross profit margin** = gross profit / net sales x 100.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Bakery A: current assets 6,00,000; current liabilities 3,00,000, so current ratio 2.0. Bakery B: 3,60,000 / 4,00,000 = 0.9, which means it may struggle to pay short-term bills. Sales 10,00,000, cost of goods sold 6,50,000: gross profit 3,50,000, margin 35%.

steps.title: Law of demand and supply
steps.body: Law of demand: price up, quantity demanded down (other things equal). Law of supply: price up, quantity supplied up. Equilibrium is where Qd = Qs. A **shift** in demand comes from income, tastes, prices of related goods, expectations; a **movement along** the curve comes only from the good's own price.

steps.title: Worked example: price ceiling
steps.body: At a ceiling of 15: Qd = 70, Qs = 50. Shortage = 20 units.

story.title: Should the cinema cut ticket prices?

scenes.text: A multiplex in Indore wonders whether a price cut will fill seats enough to raise revenue.
The answer depends on how sensitive buyers are to price.
That sensitivity is price elasticity.

steps.title: Price elasticity of demand
steps.body: Ed = % change in quantity demanded / % change in price (use absolute value). |Ed| > 1 elastic, = 1 unitary, < 1 inelastic. If demand is elastic, a price cut **raises** total revenue; if inelastic, a price cut lowers it.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Price falls from 200 to 180 (-10%) and tickets rise from 500 to 600 (+20%). Ed = 20/10 = **2** (elastic). Revenue before 200 x 500 = 1,00,000; after 180 x 600 = 1,08,000, higher as predicted.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing slope with elasticity.
- Forgetting that elasticity varies along a straight-line demand curve.

scenes.text: A print shop has fixed cost 5,000 a day plus 8 per brochure.
The owner wants to know when to accept a bulk order at a discount.
Marginal cost tells the answer.

steps.title: Cost concepts
steps.body: TC = FC + VC. AC = TC/Q. **MC = change in TC / change in Q.** In the short run MC cuts AC at the minimum of AC. A firm should accept extra output when price exceeds MC.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: TC = 5000 + 8Q. At Q = 500: TC = 9,000; AC = 18. At Q = 1000: TC = 13,000; AC = 13. MC = (13000 - 9000)/500 = **8**. A bulk order at 10 per brochure beats MC, so it adds profit.

steps.title: Structures
steps.body:
- **Perfect competition**: many sellers, identical product, price taker, free entry.
- **Monopoly**: one seller, high barriers, price maker.
- **Monopolistic competition**: many sellers, differentiated products (restaurants).
- **Oligopoly**: few firms, interdependent decisions (telecom, airlines).

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body: SI = P x r x t / 100. Amount with compound interest A = P(1 + r/100)^t.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: SI on 10,000 at 10% for 2 years = 2,000. CI: 10000 x 1.1 x 1.1 = 12,100 so interest 2,100. Difference = 100, which equals interest on the first year's interest (1000 x 10%).

scenes.text: Rent and a helper cost 60,000 a month. Each cup sells at 50 and costs 30 in ingredients.
How many cups before profit begins?
Break-even tells.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body: Contribution per unit = price - variable cost. Break-even units = fixed cost / contribution per unit. Margin of safety = actual sales - break-even sales.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Contribution = 50 - 30 = 20. Break-even = 60000 / 20 = **3,000 cups**. If the stall sells 3,800 cups, margin of safety is 800 cups and profit = 800 x 20 = 16,000.

lessons.title: Lab: Mean, median and standard deviation

scenes.text: Ravi and Sana both average 6 deals a week.
Ravi's weeks swing wildly; Sana's are steady.
Dispersion shows the difference.

steps.title: Measures
steps.body: Mean = sum/n. Median = middle value after sorting. Population standard deviation = square root of mean of squared deviations.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Data 4, 8, 6, 5, 7: mean = 30/5 = 6. Deviations -2, 2, 0, -1, 1; squares 4, 4, 0, 1, 1 sum 10; variance 2; SD = sqrt 2 = **1.41**. Median of sorted 4,5,6,7,8 = 6. Coefficient of variation = SD/mean x 100 = 23.6%.
